answer: NAB's FY25 Business & Private Banking (B&PB) growth was mostly value-accretive and broad-based, but not margin-neutral, and the latest NPL uptick is disclosed as single-name concentrated rather than systemic. Business lending grew 7.3% to $166.3bn and housing lending 5.8% to $109.3bn (results book, p.36), with the presentation stating 'Broad based growth across most sectors including Trade, Manufacturing, Construction, Transport' (IP, p.50) and segment growth of Agri +3.5%, Health +5.9%, CRE +7.4%, Other +10.4% (IP, p.50). Deposits grew 6.6%, roughly matching lending, so growth is largely self-funded. However, net interest margin fell 8bps to 3.01% 'reflecting competitive pressures impacting both the business and housing lending portfolios, as well as higher deposit costs' (results book, p.37), so net operating income (+2.1%) grew far slower than lending volumes, and opex growth (+2.9%) outpaced revenue, producing negative jaws (cost-to-income +30bps to 37.9%). Cash earnings rose only 1.6% to $3,330m. On credit quality, the FY25 impairment charge rose just 1.1% and its GLA ratio improved 1bp, with the increase 'mainly reflecting a higher charge for home lending, partially offset by a lower charge for business lending' (results book, p.37) - i.e. not driven by the fastest-growing book. Yet risk-weighted assets grew faster than loans (+9.0% vs +7.3%) due to 'growth in business lending volumes, combined with deterioration in asset quality' (results book, p.37), and business lending NPL/GLA rose to 3.22% from 2.66% a year earlier (IP, p.96/p.27). Critically, the disclosure attributes the latest half's deterioration to concentration: 'Excluding two large well secured Agri customers, underlying NPL ratio down 3bps to 3.01%,' with 'Stable to improving NPL outcomes in 2H25 for most sectors' and a book that 'remains well diversified and highly secured' (IP, p.27). Overall: the volume and revenue growth reflect genuine, broad, market-share-gaining expansion rather than credit-quality chasing, but its per-dollar profitability is thinner than the back book due to margin compression and negative jaws, and RWA/NPL metrics grew faster than volumes - a real, if largely single-name-flagged, quality cost.

key_facts.fact: Group-level, the rise in non-performing exposures was mainly driven by deterioration in the Business and Private Banking business lending portfolio, including a downgrade of a small number of large Agriculture customers.

key_facts.fact: B&PB deposits grew 6.6% to $237.9bn in FY25, roughly matching lending growth, indicating the loan growth is largely funded by the franchise rather than wholesale markets.

limitations: No standalone B&PB return-on-equity figure is disclosed; only cash earnings on average assets (1.25%, -5bps) and on average RWA (2.18%, -1bp) are given as profitability proxies.

The results book gives no dollar split of the impairment charge between B&PB housing and business lending; only qualitative direction ('higher charge for home lending, partially offset by a lower charge for business lending') is disclosed.

Sector growth rates on IP page 50 are presented on a customer-segment basis, not an industry (ANZSIC) basis, so they cannot be precisely reconciled with the ANZSIC-based NPL sector chart on IP page 27.
FY24 comparatives for B&PB were restated for a portfolio transfer between Personal Banking and B&PB and for an expense-presentation change, which limits exact like-for-like comparison.

The multi-half NPL uptrend in business lending (2.30% at Mar-24 to 3.22% at Sep-25) is only partly explained by the disclosed 'two large Agri customers' item, which addresses the most recent half only; earlier-period drivers are not itemized.

No loan-level or vintage pricing data is disclosed, so it is not possible to independently verify whether new originations carry thinner margins or weaker underwriting than the back book beyond the aggregate NIM and NPL trends shown.
